q: Does a single unimodal Gamma actually beat alternative candidate distributions (log-normal, negative-binomial, Gamma-mixture) for the per-track complexity histograms across the full LET range, or does the paper's asserted R^2 > 0.999 hide better fits that were not tabulated?
basis: The paper reports R^2 > 0.999 for a Gamma fit to all 16 monoenergetic beams, but does not compare against alternative distribution families. Physical intuition suggests that at high LET, track-core dense damage plus penumbra sparse damage could produce a bimodal complexity distribution, for which a Gamma-mixture would be more natural than a single Gamma. Raw SDD histograms would let this be tested at essentially zero extra cost, but they are not deposited.
next_steps: (1) Contact the corresponding author (Bertolet or Schuemann at MGH Physics) and request the raw SDD per-event damage-site tables for the 16 beams, or barring that, the per-beam damage-count histograms. (2) With those histograms, fit each of {Gamma, log-normal, negative-binomial, Gamma-mixture-of-2, truncated-exponential} by MLE and tabulate delta-AIC / delta-BIC per beam. (3) Explicitly check for bimodality at yF > 100 keV/mu-m via Hartigan's dip test on the raw complexity histograms.

q: Is the LET-dependence of the Gamma shape (alpha) and rate (beta) parameters really quadratic in yF, or is the quadratic a convenience fit that hides a mechanistic saturating form (like the linear-plus-saturating-exp the paper uses for SBI and BDI)?
basis: The paper fits alpha(yF) and beta(yF) as quadratics in yF but gives no mechanistic justification for that particular functional form. Notably, beta(yF) goes negative at yF ~ 175 keV/mu-m, inside the paper's own stated validity window (up to yF ~ 200 keV/mu-m for 2-MeV alphas) --- this is a diagnostic that the quadratic form is a phenomenological convenience rather than a physically-derived law. The paper uses linear-plus-saturating-exp forms for other damage-count observables (SBI, BDI), so it is asymmetric to switch to unrestricted polynomials only for the Gamma parameters.
next_steps: (1) Using the same 16-beam raw SDD histograms (once obtained), re-fit alpha(yF) and beta(yF) with candidate functional forms: {quadratic, linear+saturating-exp, Michaelis-Menten, power-law}, and compare AIC. (2) Enforce a positivity constraint on beta(yF) during meta-fit (e.g., by fitting log(beta) or by using a saturating form with a floor) and check whether the quadratic-in-log or saturating form extrapolates more sensibly to yF ~ 300 keV/mu-m (relevant for boron neutron-capture therapy alphas). (3) Publish a corrigendum or code-note documenting the yF ceiling above which the current fit becomes improper (~175 keV/mu-m).

q: Does the Gamma complexity distribution actually predict cell-survival curves for the V79-4 and irs1 lines the paper analyzes in Figure 5, if the sigmoid repair model is replaced with a more mechanistic non-homologous-end-joining (NHEJ) / homologous-recombination (HR) partition model?
basis: The paper itself describes the sigmoid repair model used to convert complexity distributions into cell survival as 'qualitative' (paper text). The RBE-vs-LET curves in Figure 5 are therefore a weak downstream test of the Gamma-complexity hypothesis. If the true test is 'does the Gamma complexity distribution carry the physically-relevant information for survival prediction,' a mechanistic repair model (e.g., MCNP-DNA + PARTRAC's kinetic NHEJ/HR module, or the LEM-IV local-effect-model repair) is needed.
next_steps: (1) Take the reproduced Gamma complexity distributions per beam (per this replication) and couple them into a mechanistic repair model --- e.g., use McMahon et al.'s Medras kinetic model (open source, github.com/sjmcmahon/Medras-MC) which takes damage complexity as input and produces survival curves. (2) Compare Medras-predicted vs paper's-sigmoid-predicted RBE-vs-LET curves against the same V79-4 and irs1 experimental data (Hill 2004, Jones 1987). (3) If Medras + Gamma-complexity predicts survival better than sigmoid + Gamma-complexity, that strengthens the case that the Gamma-complexity distribution is capturing physically-relevant information (rather than a coincidence of the fit).

q: How sensitive are the fitted (alpha, beta) values to the choice of scoring-volume geometry (1 um sphere) --- would a 100 nm cylinder mimicking a nucleosome, or a 5 um sphere mimicking a whole nucleus, give a materially different Gamma parameterization?
basis: The paper fixes the scoring volume as a 1 um-diameter sphere throughout (this is the volume over which lineal energy y is computed and over which damage sites are aggregated into 'complexity per track'). But complexity of damage is inherently a scale-dependent concept: nucleosome-scale (100 nm) clustering picks up track-core physics, whereas nucleus-scale (5+ um) aggregation smears over multiple independent tracks. The paper does not report a sensitivity study across scoring-volume sizes, so it is unknown whether the Gamma family is robust across scales or is a coincidence of the 1 um choice.
next_steps: (1) Re-run TOPAS-nBio for a single reference beam (say 4-MeV alpha, yF ~ 95 keV/mu-m) with three scoring-volume diameters: 100 nm, 1 um (baseline), 5 um. (2) Fit the resulting per-track damage-complexity histograms with a Gamma and record R^2 + (alpha, beta) per scale. (3) If the Gamma family remains R^2 > 0.99 across all three scales but (alpha, beta) shift systematically, that is a strong result --- publish a scale-transformation law. If the Gamma family breaks down at one extreme (e.g., 100 nm becomes bimodal), that is also a strong result --- it bounds the physical regime of the Gamma model.

q: Can the Gamma-complexity model be validated directly against plasmid DSB-yield experiments (much cleaner, ex-cellulo, no repair confound), rather than only against cell-survival experiments that convolve the complexity distribution with an unknown repair sigmoid?
basis: Plasmid DNA irradiation experiments (e.g., pUC19 or pBR322 in aqueous solution under proton/alpha beams) produce clean measurements of SSB and DSB yields per Gy per Da of DNA, without any repair-model confound. Milligan, Ward, and others published such data at multiple LETs in the 1990s-2010s. These would be a direct testbed for the Gamma-complexity distribution's predicted N_sites_with_DSB per track and the ratio of complex-DSB to simple-DSB. The paper does not test against any plasmid data, only cell data (Figure 5).
next_steps: (1) Curate a small dataset of published plasmid DSB-yield vs LET measurements (Milligan JR et al., Radiat Res 1993; Fulford et al., Int J Radiat Biol 2001; Belli et al. plasmid irradiation series). (2) For each plasmid experiment's beam parameters, compute yF using standard microdosimetry, then use MGM to predict N_sites_with_DSB per track and the complex-to-simple DSB ratio. (3) Compare predicted vs measured yields. (4) If MGM reproduces the plasmid data within experimental error across the LET range, that is a strong, repair-free validation of the Gamma-complexity model. If it does not, that isolates the failure to the biological repair layer rather than the physics-of-damage layer.
